headline_hi: हौसले से जीती ज़िंदगी की जंग
headline_en: Won the Battle of Life with Courage
summary_en: The story of thirty-eight-year-old Shijoy Jacob from Mumbai gives us all great courage. Shijoy was born with a foot condition called clubfoot. In his childhood, both his feet were turned inward. His mother Pushpa used to take him to hospitals in Mumbai for treatment. One doctor had even put plaster casts on both his legs. But Shijoy never let this problem get in the way of his dreams. Today, that same Shijoy has cycled hundreds of kilometers across several countries. In the year 2026, he went on a cycling journey from Cambodia to Vietnam with three friends. Throughout this entire journey, they had no support vehicle with them. He carried his own luggage and fixed punctures himself. He has cycled in India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia. Not only that, he has also completed a fifteen-thousand-foot trek in the Himalayas.

lead.title: ‘I Struggled To Walk’: Born With Clubfoot, 38-YO Has Cycled Across 4 Countries & Trekked to 15000 Ft
lead.summary: Whenever Shijoy Jacob leaves home for a cycling expedition, his mother, Pushpa, worries about his return. “I feel scared when he goes,” she says. “I don’t even want to sleep until he comes back.” She remembers a time when her son struggled to walk. Today, she watches him set off on journeys that take him hundreds of kilometres away from home, sometimes across international borders. In 2026, Shijoy, 38, was pedalling from Cambodia into Vietnam with three friends. There was no support vehicle following them. They carried their own luggage, repaired their own punctures and sometimes cycled more than 100 kilometres in a day. Along the way, they stopped for tea and meals, taking their time to explore the places they passed. But growing up in Mumbai, Shijoy had once wondered whether he would even be able to run alongside his friends. Pushpa once took her son to hospitals so he could walk comfortably. Today, she watches him cycle across countries and trek in the Himalayas. “I was born different, but I don’t think that should define me and stop my dreams,” he says. “If I have thought of any goal, it should be achieved.” Today, Shijoy has cycled through India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and trekked to 15,000 feet in the Himalayas. ‘Will I be able to do it?’ Shijoy was born in Mumbai with a congenital limb deformity, commonly referred to as clubfoot or congenital talipes equinovarus. Both his legs were twisted inward, with the left more severely affected. When he was born, his parents took him to doctors in Mumbai. headline_en: Mosque Loudspeakers to Give Earthquake Warnings
summary_en: A unique initiative has been taken in Indonesia to save people's lives from natural disasters. Here, mosque loudspeakers will now serve to give earthquake warnings. This brilliant plan was created by a team of researchers from Japan and Indonesia. Dr. Inoue Hiroshi of Kyoto University thought of this during research in Sumatra. There are millions of mosques in Indonesia, and loudspeakers are installed everywhere. This pilot project is being run for five years until the year 2030. These speakers are being connected to a sensor network that measures ground movement. The alarm will sound on the loudspeakers before the strong tremors of an earthquake arrive. Often, mobile networks suddenly fail during major earthquakes. But mosque speakers are managed by local people and are always operational. In some mosques, this system has already been successfully integrated.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The hardest part of any early warning system isn’t the science. It’s finding infrastructure that reaches everyone, holds up under pressure, and gets maintained over years by the people who depend on it. In Indonesia, a team of Japanese and Indonesian researchers think that infrastructure already exists. It broadcasts the call to prayer five times a day. With the largest Muslim population in the world, Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques, nearly all equipped with loudspeakers that reach the surrounding community. A five-year pilot project running until 2030 is testing whether those speakers can double as earthquake alert klaxons, connected to a seismic sensor network that sounds an alarm before the shaking arrives. Several mosques have already been hooked up. The project was conceived by Dr. Inoue Hiroshi of the Disaster Prevention Research Institute at Kyoto University, who came up with the idea while researching deadly earthquakes in Sumatra nearly two decades ago. “Every community has a mosque,” he told the Guardian . The rest of his argument was practical: “The advantage of a mosque speaker is that they’re existing and well maintained. For any disaster infrastructure, maintenance is the big challenge… but the mosque speaker is maintained by the people.” Mobile phones are the default tool for modern disaster alerts, but phone networks can fail in an earthquake. Mosque loudspeakers, tested five times a day by the communities that run them, are harder to knock out. The seconds that matter in an earthquake Earthquake early warning is different from tsunami warning. Tsunamis build over time and can be tracked; communities might have minutes or hours to act. headline_hi: छात्रों ने छेड़ी प्लास्टिक मुक्ति मुहिम
headline_en: Students Launch Campaign to Eliminate Plastic
summary_en: Schoolchildren around the world are now stepping forward against plastic waste. In a school in Singapore, two thousand students used a heavy amount of plastic every year. Seeing this problem, fifteen to sixteen-year-old children took a big step. They joined a special campaign called the Unplastify Challenge from Latin America. The children of Singapore promoted reusable lunch boxes in the school. For this wonderful effort, they won the first prize in the year 2026. Over the past eight years, four hundred schools from twenty-five countries have joined this movement. More than three thousand students have together prevented seventy-two tons of plastic waste. Students from Chile created a biodegradable glitter to replace plastic. In Costa Rica, children used natural loofahs instead of plastic sponges. Meanwhile, teenagers in Türkiye have researched safer alternatives to medical gloves.

lead.title: Teenagers Worldwide Are Tackling the Plastics Crisis
lead.summary: W hen students in Singapore looked around their school cafeteria, they could see a problem shared all over the world: Single-use Styrofoam was ubiquitous. They soon learned that the school’s 2,000 students used 72,000 pieces of Styrofoam and other types of plastic every year. To find a solution, they joined the Unplastify Challenge , a global movement initiated by the Latin American social enterprise Unplastify and funded by the National Geographic Society, a nonprofit that seeks to foster environmental stewardship. What makes the program unique is its audience, design and scope. Teenagers, usually 15 to 16 years old, design and implement solutions to “unplastify” their schools, communities, neighborhoods and homes. In Singapore, the students decided to campaign for multi-use lunch boxes, winning them first place in the Unplastify Challenge 2026, the 12th such event of its kind. A garbage-strewn beach in Bali, Indonesia. Unless effective action is taken, it’s predicted that global plastic production will more than double over the next 15 years. Credit: Mariia Ploshikhina / Shutterstock In the eight years since it began, Unplastify has worked with over 3,000 students at 400 schools in 25 countries, mostly in Latin America, but also in Africa, Asia, North America and Europe. Together these students have come up with over 1,000 strategies, leading efforts to avoid an estimated 72 tons of plastic. In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter, thus avoiding four kilos of plastic in a single year. In Costa Rica, students have replaced plastic sponges with natural luffa. headline_en: Safaris Resume in Indravati Tiger Reserve
summary_en: Good news has arrived for nature lovers from Chhattisgarh's Indravati Tiger Reserve. After a long wait of forty years, safaris are starting here once again. Located in Bastar's Bijapur district, this forest became a tiger reserve in 1983. Due to security issues in that area, visits by tourists were completely stopped. Even the forest department team could not go inside for monitoring. Now, with conditions improving, the government is opening it from November 1, 2026. This vast reserve is spread across approximately two thousand eight hundred square kilometers. Many magnificent wild animals such as tigers, leopards, bears, and deer live safely here. Chhattisgarh's state animal, the rare wild water buffalo, is also found here. According to the forest department, six tigers are recorded here, and a new count is underway. With improved security, officials are now able to patrol the entire forest easily.

lead.title: This Chhattisgarh Tiger Reserve Is Reopening for Safaris After 40 Years: Spot Tigers & Rare Otters
lead.summary: For nearly 40 years, wildlife lovers could visit tiger reserves across India, but organised safaris at Indravati in Chhattisgarh remained out of reach. The reason was not a lack of wildlife. It was the danger of travelling through the forest. Located in Bastar's Bijapur district, Indravati was declared a tiger reserve in 1983. But as Maoist insurgency and armed conflict affected the region, travelling through large parts of the forest became risky. Even forest officials struggled to reach certain areas for patrolling and wildlife monitoring. With safety a major concern, organised tourism remained suspended for nearly four decades. Now, that is beginning to change. As security conditions improve, the Chhattisgarh forest department is preparing to welcome tourists again, with 1 November 2026 announced as the target reopening date. For visitors, it could mean the chance to finally explore a forest that has remained largely outside India's wildlife tourism circuit. But what makes Indravati worth discovering after all these years? What has remained hidden from tourists for 40 years? Spread across 2,799 sq km, Indravati is one of Central India's largest tiger reserves. Its forests shelter tigers, leopards, sloth bears, gaurs, wild dogs and deer. It is also an important habitat for the endangered wild water buffalo, Chhattisgarh's state animal. Indravati's long absence from the tourism circuit has also meant that parts of its wildlife remain poorly documented. Photograph: (deccanchronicle)   According to figures presented by the forest department, the reserve has six tigers, although a fresh population assessment is underway. headline_en: Libraries to Stay Open Even at Night
summary_en: Libraries in rural areas of America have launched a new facility for people. The library in the city of Wyoming, Minnesota, now stays open even after closing hours. East Central Regional Library has named this special program Extended Access. Through this, people can go inside and study even without any staff present. According to library director Carla Lydon, this is very helpful for working people. Those who remain busy during the day can come here at night. Local author Michael Sion sits here to work on his new novel. He says that he fills out job applications and important documents here comfortably. Even on scorching summer days, this place offers relief to people. Such an arrangement has also started in several other states like Utah and California. This small change is making access to books much easier for ordinary people.

lead.title: The Library Is Closed. Feel Free to Come In.
lead.summary: This story was originally published in the Daily Yonder. For more rural reporting and small-town stories visit dailyyonder.com . For Michael Sayen, visiting the local library after hours is a great way to get work done, or seek respite from the weather, regardless of what day it is. “We just had Labor Day, the library is closed all day. But if you have extended hours, you can come in and do the work, or cool down from a hot day or whatever you need to do,” Sayen said the day after Labor Day while working on a novel at the Wyoming, Minnesota branch of the East Central Regional Library (ECRL) in Chisago County. Sayen, who lives in nearby Forest Lake north of Minneapolis, adds that he has found after-hours access useful for filing time-sensitive job applications or court documents. Michael Sayen uses a computer at the Wyoming Giese Memorial Library to work on a novel. Sayen is a user of the Extended Access program at the Wyoming Library. Credit: H. Jiahong Pan/Daily Yonder The Wyoming branch library is home to a new ECRL initiative called “extended access,” which allows users to access a library branch when it is unstaffed. “We hope that it allows more people to use the facility, in particular those who may not be able to get to the library during otherwise limited hours due to work and family schedules,” ECRL executive director Carla Lydon wrote in an email. ECRL is one of a handful of rural library systems across the United States to offer such a service, increasing library access at a time when libraries are struggling for funding. How it works Extended access goes by many names depending on location. The Summit County Library in Utah calls it extended access hours . headline_en: Health Benefits of Japanese Sweet Potato
summary_en: Japanese sweet potato is being widely liked for its distinct flavor and nutrition. Its skin is reddish-purple, and the inside is completely white and creamy. Compared to regular sweet potatoes, it is sweeter and richer in taste. According to dietitian Danielle, it can help provide energy to active people. One serving contains about twenty-six grams of carbs and four grams of fiber. Dietitian Alissa Smolen explains that its fiber can keep the stomach full for a long time. Orange sweet potatoes contain vitamin A, whereas Japanese sweet potatoes have more vitamin C. Vitamin E and special anthocyanin compounds are also found in abundance in it. This is the same nutrient that is also found in blueberries and red cabbage. Experts advise eating it paired with protein and healthy fats. Eating both types of sweet potatoes can provide the body with different nutrients.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: What sets Japanese sweet potatoes apart, nutritionally speaking
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve bought a Japanese sweet potato, cut into it expecting orange, and found creamy white instead, you’ve already spotted the first thing that sets it apart. The skin is reddish-purple, the flesh is ivory, and the flavor is sweeter and earthier than the orange kinds most of us grew up with. The nutrition is different too, so the difference isn’t just skin deep. What Japanese sweet potatoes bring to the table They have about 26 grams of carbohydrates per 103-gram serving, nine percent of the daily value for adults. But unlike a plain starch, they come with fiber, potassium, and vitamin C alongside. Registered dietitian Danielle Smiley of NutriDS, LLC notes they’re well-suited for people who are physically active: the carbohydrates fuel effort and help with recovery. Registered dietitian Alyssa Smolen puts the fiber at about four grams per serving, which is enough to keep you full for a while. She suggests building them into a meal with a protein and some healthy fat rather than eating them on their own. What about orange sweet potatoes? Orange sweet potatoes are high in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A. Japanese ones run higher in vitamins C and E and carry more anthocyanins, the same pigments behind the color in blueberries and red cabbage. Research on different varieties shows considerable variation in carotenoids, flavonoids, and other plant compounds depending on flesh color. If you eat both types across the week, you get more of that range. They’re doing different things, basically.
